column1:
An EDR anomaly engine fires at 02:14 local time with 64% confidence. The user's baseline shows they routinely work overnight. What is the right next step?

A. Run the other three validation checks before deciding.
B. Close it. The overnight baseline already explains the timing.
C. Escalate now. Activity at 02:14 on an anomaly alert is suspicious enough.
D. Decode the command line in full before doing anything else.
column2:
A. Run the other three validation checks before deciding.

The user's overnight baseline speaks to one validation check: environmental context. Agreement on one check is not validation. Technical fidelity, threat intelligence, and business impact are still unchecked; check all four, then decide. The 64% is the engine reporting how unusual the activity is, not a verdict on whether it is malicious; it does not stand in for the other three checks. And if context does clear it, the close is a benign true positive, not a false positive: the engine saw a real deviation.

column1:
Two alerts land at once, and you can open only one in the next 15 minutes. Alert 1: a lobby kiosk laptop with no sensitive access, where an Office-to-PowerShell chain is corroborated by a proxy record and a beacon is still running. Alert 2: a domain controller with a single low-confidence anomaly, a login at an unusual hour and nothing else. Which do you open first?

A. Alert 2. Criticality always wins: a domain controller outranks any kiosk.
B. Alert 2. The weak signal on the critical host has the larger blast radius.
C. Neither until both are validated; picking one now would be guesswork.
D. Alert 1. A corroborated chain with a live beacon is uncontained activity.
column2:
D. Alert 1. A corroborated chain with a live beacon is uncontained activity.

Criticality weighs how much an alert matters if it is real; it does not make a weak signal strong. Alert 1 is malicious activity corroborated by an independent record and not contained by any control: the beacon is still running. That meets escalation criterion 1 on any host, so the escalation tripwire applies whatever the host's criticality. Alert 2 comes next, and its criticality is why it should not wait long, but a single unusual-hour login is an anomaly to validate, not an intrusion in progress. In a post-mortem, leaving a live beacon running to look at a lone anomaly is the choice you could not defend.

column1:
An adversary uses living-off-the-land binaries with no custom malware. Which detection approach is built to catch this, and what form does it usually take in practice?

A. Signature-based: the binaries' hashes will match threat-intelligence indicators.
B. Anomaly-based: each single LOLBin execution deviates far enough from baseline to flag.
C. Behavioral: the sequence is the artifact, often encoded as a hand-written rule.
D. Rule-based only: a hand-written rule cannot be behavioral, so that label does not apply.
column2:
C. Behavioral: the sequence is the artifact, often encoded as a hand-written rule.

Every binary in the chain is signed and individually unremarkable, so hashes match nothing bad and single events sit inside tolerance. What is detectable is the sequence: the parent-child chain and its context. The family label can be plural here: a deterministic Sigma-style rule that encodes that chain is rule-based by construction and behavioral by content. Name both when both apply; what matters for triage is reading the logic that fired, not picking its one true family.

column1:
A signature engine reports an exact match on a known-bad SHA-256. At the same moment, a UEBA (user and entity behavior analytics) engine flags the same host for 'unusual process activity'. Before any investigation, how should the analyst calibrate trust in the two signals?

A. Treat both equally: every alert deserves identical skepticism until it is validated.
B. The signature hit starts with the higher prior; the anomaly needs corroboration.
C. Trust the anomaly more: it is learned from this environment, and signatures are generic.
D. Trust whichever engine was tuned most recently, since it reflects current technique.
column2:
B. The signature hit starts with the higher prior; the anomaly needs corroboration.

This is the trust-calibration posture from the detection-mechanisms page. The mechanism label sets a prior, not a verdict. An exact indicator match starts higher because it is precise about the artifact, but turning that prior into confidence requires the calibration facts: is the indicator fresh, from a credible source, and rare here, or a stale hash on a dual-use tool? The anomaly is genuine signal that stays ambiguous until something corroborates it. Either way, the label is a prompt to read the logic that fired, not proof.

column1:
An alert reports an outbound TLS connection to a domain registered three days ago. The process is signed certutil.exe. The user is a developer. What would most raise your confidence that this is malicious?

A. Domain age, certutil, and no documented build process that downloads with certutil.
B. The domain age alone. Domains registered within a week are suspicious enough to act on.
C. The process alone. certutil making any outbound TLS connection is enough to act on.
D. Domain age plus the TLS encryption. Encrypted traffic to a new domain hides the payload.
column2:
A. Domain age, certutil, and no documented build process that downloads with certutil.

In this environment each signal is weak alone: new domains and certutil both have benign uses (certutil fetches CRLs and certificate updates). The combination of a new domain, a download utility this user has no reason to run, and no documented business reason is the classic certutil-as-LOLBin pattern. That combination is what raises confidence, not any single signal. TLS adds nothing: most outbound traffic is encrypted, so it does not separate malicious connections from benign ones.

column1:
An EDR alert shows: powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0ATwBiAGoAZQBjAHQA... What does -enc tell you, and what is the right parsing move?

A. The payload is encrypted. Without the key, judge the alert on the parent process alone.
B. The flag itself is the verdict. -enc only exists for attackers, so this is a true positive.
C. The flag is administrative noise. Plenty of vendor tooling uses -enc; drop it from the parse.
D. The payload is Base64 of UTF-16LE text. Decode it, then judge the decoded command.
column2:
D. The payload is Base64 of UTF-16LE text. Decode it, then judge the decoded command.

-EncodedCommand takes a Base64-encoded UTF-16LE string. That is an encoding, not encryption, so it decodes locally with no key. The surrounding flags (-nop, -w hidden, abbreviated names) raise suspicion, and legitimate automation does use -enc, which is exactly why the decoded payload, not the flag, decides. Here the decoded text begins with IEX and New-Object, the classic download-and-execute-in-memory prefix.

column1:
A parsed process tree reads: explorer.exe → WINWORD.EXE → msdt.exe. A second branch on the same host shows svchost.exe → sdiagnhost.exe → conhost.exe. Which link is the anomaly?

A. explorer.exe → WINWORD.EXE. Word should be launched by the Office click-to-run service.
B. svchost.exe → sdiagnhost.exe. A service host should never launch a scripted diagnostics host.
C. WINWORD.EXE → msdt.exe. A document reader spawning a diagnostic tool is the anomaly.
D. None. Every process in both branches is a signed Microsoft binary, so all of it is expected.
column2:
C. WINWORD.EXE → msdt.exe. A document reader spawning a diagnostic tool is the anomaly.

Explorer launching Word is a normal user double-click. svchost.exe launching sdiagnhost.exe (the Scripted Diagnostics host) with a conhost.exe child is how Windows normally runs troubleshooters. The break in the story is the middle link of the first branch: a word processor has no business spawning the Microsoft Support Diagnostic Tool, and that parent-child pair is the signature of the Follina exploit (CVE-2022-30190). In a live Follina case the payload then appears as a shell or LOLBin child of sdiagnhost.exe, which is the second place to look. Every node being signed by Microsoft is exactly why lineage, not identity, is what you parse. Follina was patched in 2022 and Microsoft has deprecated MSDT itself, but the lesson outlives the bug: an Office application spawning a system utility is the anomaly to parse for, whatever the utility.

column1:
An analyst pivots to Windows Security Event 4688 to reconstruct process creations, but the CommandLine field is blank on every event. What is the most likely reason?

A. The activity was fileless, so there were no command lines to record in the event.
B. Command-line capture is a separate policy setting, off by default and never enabled.
C. The attacker selectively cleared the field, which is why the rest of the event survived.
D. Event 4688 has no command-line field at all; only Sysmon Event 1 can record one.
column2:
B. Command-line capture is a separate policy setting, off by default and never enabled.

4688 does have a CommandLine field, but populating it requires the Group Policy setting 'Include command line in process creation events' (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Audit Process Creation), which is off by default, on top of the Audit Process Creation audit policy that makes 4688 fire at all. If it was never enabled, every historical event is blank and no retroactive fix exists. It is a telemetry gap you discover exactly when you need the data. The compensating sources are EDR process telemetry and Sysmon Event 1 (now also a built-in optional feature on Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025), and only if they were already running when the activity happened. This is why parsing includes knowing what your telemetry was configured to capture.

column1:
An identity provider flags a session token for a sales manager, presented from a new hosting-provider ASN with no sign-in prompt. Twelve minutes later the mail tenant's audit log records a new inbox rule on her mailbox. No host or process appears in either record. What should you join the two events on?

A. The account plus the session ID carried in both the sign-in and the audit record.
B. The source IP alone. If both records show one address, they are the same actor.
C. Timestamp proximity. Two events on one account within 30 minutes belong together.
D. The MFA result. An MFA-satisfied sign-in earlier that day means the session is hers.
column2:
A. The account plus the session ID carried in both the sign-in and the audit record.

With no host or PID in the story, the account and the session are the join keys. A session ID that appears on both records ties the replayed token to the action taken with it. A shared IP is weaker: addresses change with proxies and VPNs, and unrelated users can share one. Timing alone joins coincidences, and tenant audit records can arrive in the SIEM long after the event, so read event time, not arrival time. MFA satisfied proves a human authenticated once; it says nothing about who presented the token afterward, which is exactly how a stolen session is used. The cloud and identity parsing page covers this join.

column1:
A rule fires on exactly the behavior it describes: a signed backup agent reads every file in a user's home directory and uploads over TLS. Validation shows the agent is approved, deployed by IT, and behaving as its vendor documents. How should the alert be recorded?

A. False positive (logic): the rule matched something it was never meant to match.
B. False positive (data): bad telemetry made a normal agent look like exfiltration.
C. True positive on detection, authorized on activity: a benign true positive.
D. Undetermined: approved software can still be abused, so no call is possible yet.
column2:
C. True positive on detection, authorized on activity: a benign true positive.

The detection did its job: the behavior it describes really happened. On the detection axis that is a true positive, and the activity axis records why it is not a threat: authorized, which ASSURED calls a benign true positive. A false positive means the rule matched something it was not meant to match (logic) or fired on bad telemetry (data); neither is the case here. The label matters downstream: a benign true positive is cleared by context (a pattern entry or a scoped, expiring exception) and the rule stays as written, while a false positive is a defect in the rule or the data. Record the evidence that showed the activity was authorized, so the close stays defensible.

column1:
On a managed macOS developer laptop, a behavioral EDR rule fires: Cursor Helper (Plugin), the IDE's extension host, launched a child process that opened TLS connections. The binary is signed with the vendor's Developer ID and notarized. Which parsed field moves the investigation forward most?

A. The signing status. A notarized vendor binary settles the question on its own.
B. The child's script path, which shows which extension or bundle code actually ran.
C. The parent name. Cursor Helper (Plugin) is an IDE process, so the chain is expected.
D. The destination port. Traffic on port 443 is normal and needs no further parsing.
column2:
B. The child's script path, which shows which extension or bundle code actually ran.

The IDE runs extension code, MCP servers and agent commands under the vendor's signature, so the signature, the parent name, and the port all describe the container, not the code. The child's script path (inside the signed app bundle, in a user-writable directory, or in a third-party extension folder) is what tells you which code launched the connections. It also points to the next lookups: the extension inventory, the MDM record for the installed version and hash, and the destinations against the vendor's published allowlist. Signed and notarized proves who published the binary, not what it ran.

column1:
A draft Alert handoff reads: 'Validated alert: encoded PowerShell from Word, beacon to a new domain, corroborated by proxy logs. Recommendation: isolate the host and reset the user's password.' What is the main problem with it?

A. Nothing. A containment recommendation is the most useful thing Alert can hand to IR.
B. It is too long. A handoff should name the alert and leave everything else to Subject.
C. It names the evidence source. Proxy logs belong in Uncover, not in the Alert handoff.
D. Containment replaced the leads and flags, and the escalation tripwire went unchecked.
column2:
D. Containment replaced the leads and flags, and the escalation tripwire went unchecked.

Alert hands forward the validated alert, leads for Subject and Uncover (including the working hypothesis and known gaps), and flags for Scope, Risk, and Escalation. This draft skips the leads and flags and puts a containment plan in their place. Unless the alert closes at intake (a Level 0 pattern close, or a no-signal false-positive close), the verdict belongs to later phases, and containment always does. Here the evidence describes confirmed malicious activity that no control has contained, so the flag that matters is escalation criterion 1, met: the escalation tripwire fires, IR is paged, evidence is preserved, and only pre-authorized actions run. A password reset needs IR approval. A confirmed escalation criterion escalates from any phase, but escalation is a handoff, not a verdict.

column1:
In Case C, rvega's password has been reset and an admin has revoked all of her refresh tokens. Which entity still holds a standing path into her mailbox?

A. The replayed session S2. A session cookie outlives both a password reset and token revocation.
B. None. Revoking every refresh token she holds cuts all access tied to her account at once.
C. The consented OAuth app. Its grant survives user-focused actions until someone removes it.
D. Her laptop. The device that opened the lure page still holds a cached sign-in to the tenant.
column2:
C. The consented OAuth app. Its grant survives user-focused actions until someone removes it.

The consented application is a separate identity with its own grant. A password reset does not reliably revoke what it holds. Revoking her refresh tokens cuts the tokens it already has (issued access tokens still run until they expire), but the consent grant itself stays until someone removes it, ready for the next token the app obtains. That is why Case C gives the app its own containment line. The replayed session was revoked and refused, and the laptop was examined and cleared: a witness, not a subject. The broader lesson is that identity is plural. Behind any named user sit sessions, application grants, service accounts and federated identities, and Subject profiles all of them, not just the one the alert named.

column1:
A user's action maps cleanly to their assigned role, so the authorization dimension looks fine at a glance. Why does it still reward a second look?

A. The role may be wrong: toxic permission pairs and recent role changes hide behind a clean mapping.
B. It does not. Once the action maps to the role, authorization is answered and the analyst moves on.
C. Because authorization data is usually stale, the behavioral baseline should be checked in its place.
D. Because authorization only covers human accounts, service accounts need a separate relationship pass.
column2:
A. The role may be wrong: toxic permission pairs and recent role changes hide behind a clean mapping.

'The action maps to the role' answers the shallow question. The deeper ones are whether the role is right for this person now, whether it changed recently, and whether individually reasonable permissions combine into an unsafe pairing. Those gaps sit exactly where the first glance says everything is fine.

column1:
A service account suddenly logs in interactively at 02:30. Which entity type pattern does this match?

A. Normal. Service accounts authenticate constantly; the hour is only unusual for humans.
B. A policy violation for the account owner to fix, but not itself security-relevant.
C. Probably the on-call engineer running a manual test with the service account's credentials.
D. A compromise signal. Service accounts are non-interactive by design; this is near-canonical.
column2:
D. A compromise signal. Service accounts are non-interactive by design; this is near-canonical.

Service accounts have predictable, non-interactive behavior by design, which makes an interactive login a high-confidence Subject signal: the credential is being used outside its designed lane. It is a signal, not proof. An emergency-access (break-glass) procedure or an admin troubleshooting with the service credential produces the same event, so the next check is who initiated the session and whether a sanctioned reason (a change ticket, an emergency-access record) exists.

column1:
An egress alert flags a workstation making sustained connections to an external host on port 443. What is the entity-type question to ask about this network identifier?

A. Whether the traffic really is the protocol 443 implies; SSH or DNS on 443 is the bypass.
B. How rare port 443 is in the environment. Uncommon ports are the primary tunneling signal.
C. Whether the destination IP has a clean reputation. A clean score clears the connection.
D. None yet. Protocol analysis is deep-evidence work that belongs to Uncover, not Subject.
column2:
A. Whether the traffic really is the protocol 443 implies; SSH or DNS on 443 is the bypass.

Port 443 is the most common port on the internet, so rarity carries no signal at all. The signal is protocol/port mismatch: traffic on 443 that is not actually TLS, or DNS on an arbitrary high port, is the classic bypass pattern, because attackers pick common ports precisely to blend in. Reputation helps but does not clear anything; a clean destination means only that it has not been caught yet. And conformance cuts one way only: most command-and-control (C2) traffic rides genuine TLS on 443, so conformant traffic moves the question to destination age, certificate, JA4 TLS client fingerprint and connection periodicity.

column1:
In ASSURED's vocabulary, what separates insider risk from insider threat?

A. Nothing. The two terms are interchangeable vocabulary for any insider case.
B. Risk is possible harm regardless of intent; threat is intentional, shown by evidence.
C. Severity tiers: risk describes low-severity cases, threat describes high-severity ones.
D. Direction: insider risk comes from inside, insider threat from outside partners.
column2:
B. Risk is possible harm regardless of intent; threat is intentional, shown by evidence.

The distinction is about intent. Most insider risk is unintentional (mistakes, workarounds, policy violations). Insider threat is intentional, and the methodology reserves that designation for cases where evidence supports it. Two calibrations: the label is a revisable hypothesis, not a verdict (and the split is a practitioner convention: NIST and CISA define insider threat to include acts done wittingly or unwittingly, so map it to your organization's vocabulary), and the label shapes who gets engaged, never whether confirmed harmful activity gets a response. Containment and escalation trigger on act, asset, and impact; intent is resolved in parallel.

column1:
An engineer's activity is consistent with their own 90-day baseline but looks nothing like anyone else's in the same role. What is the best reading?

A. Their own baseline clears it. Per-entity comparison is the framework's primary question.
B. The peer mismatch overrides the personal baseline. Escalate on the role comparison alone.
C. Peer comparison across engineers is noise. Roles vary too much for the mismatch to matter.
D. The gap between the two baselines is itself a signal; investigate what explains it.
column2:
D. The gap between the two baselines is itself a signal; investigate what explains it.

Per-entity baselining is the framework's headline question, and here it passes. But the framework also runs the peer-group comparison, and when the two disagree, the disagreement is informative: it can mean a legitimately unusual job, or a baseline that was poisoned by long-running compromise before the window began. Neither baseline overrides the other; the gap between them is what deserves the look.

column1:
An insider bulk-exports a customer database, then clears their shell history and deletes the staged archive. Under the Insider Threat Matrix, where does the history-clearing evidence belong?

A. Motive. Hiding the activity reveals why the insider acted in the first place.
B. Means. Shell access is the capability that made the whole export possible.
C. Anti-forensics. Destroying evidence of the act after the fact is its own section.
D. Preparation. Cleanup is part of setting up the operation so it survives later scrutiny.
column2:
C. Anti-forensics. Destroying evidence of the act after the fact is its own section.

The matrix organizes insider tradecraft into sections: motive (why), means (what made it possible), preparation (setting it up), infringement (the harmful act, here the bulk export), and anti-forensics (concealing or destroying evidence afterward). History-clearing and deleting staged archives are textbook anti-forensics, and their presence upgrades the case: deliberate evidence destruction is among the strongest intent signals available. It still gets verified rather than assumed: scheduled cleanup jobs, retention scripts, and shell configurations that trim history all exist, so the analyst confirms the mechanism was manual before treating the cleanup as a confession.

column1:
A marketing team under deadline converted confidential documents into image files to get them past a slow secure file-sharing tool and shared them externally, exposing customer data. What does Subject classify this as?

A. Insider risk: no intent to harm. The exposure is still contained and assessed for notification; the fix is process.
B. Insider threat. Customer data was deliberately moved outside the boundary, so intent is irrelevant to the label.
C. Neither. Exposure through an approved sharing channel is a DLP tuning problem for engineering, not a Subject question.
D. Undetermined. Hold both the label and the response until interviews with the team establish what they intended.
column2:
A. Insider risk: no intent to harm. The exposure is still contained and assessed for notification; the fix is process.

Insider risk is the right label: the workaround was a deliberate act with no intent to harm, aimed at getting work done past a slow tool, not at stealing data. But the label only decides the long-term fix, not the immediate response. Customer data left the boundary through a deliberate control bypass, so the exposure is scoped and contained, the regulatory notification question is asked (a notification clock does not care about motive), and the DLP bypass is recorded as a confirmed policy violation. Holding the response until intent is known gets the order backward: the label can wait, the exposure cannot. What the risk classification changes is what happens after: process improvement, a faster approved sharing path, instead of an enforcement action that would add friction without fixing the cause. (The scenario is an illustrative composite, not a published incident.)

column1:
On a developer's macOS laptop, a signed IDE helper process runs with its sandbox disabled and makes encrypted outbound calls. A behavioral EDR rule maps the pattern to Empire-style post-exploitation tradecraft. What should Subject do before reaching a verdict?

A. Block and contain immediately. An Empire-pattern match on a developer host is conclusive.
B. Read context first: signing, install record, extension layer, peer baseline, then verdict.
C. Isolate the device and hold it for a forensic image before touching any other dimension.
D. Close it. A signed, notarized binary from a known vendor is sufficient on its own to clear.
column2:
B. Read context first: signing, install record, extension layer, peer baseline, then verdict.

A behavioral pattern match alone is not Subject's verdict. The four dimensions plus access scope plus operational risk produce the picture. A signed, MDM-installed, peer-baselined binary running in a documented configuration on a developer workstation reads very differently from the same activity from an unsigned binary in a user-writable directory. Subject's job is to record that distinction defensibly, not to react to the pattern match alone. Even a benign verdict carries caveats: the signature covers the editor, not the extensions, MCP servers and workspace tasks it runs, and developer workstations hide persistence in IDE extensions, dotfiles, and package-manager hooks, so the close records what was checked.

column1:
An HR referral asks whether a departing engineer's account moved data to personal storage. EDR and the CASB agree on what happened. Which line belongs in the case ticket?

A. Account jkessler, a disgruntled engineer, uploaded 2.3 GB to personal storage before leaving.
B. HR says the owner of account jkessler is under stress at home; the background is attached.
C. Referral IRP-2026-0412 received; collection waits until HR explains why it suspects him.
D. Account jkessler uploaded a 2.3 GB file to personal-drive[.]example, 22:47 to 22:52 UTC.
column2:
D. Account jkessler uploaded a 2.3 GB file to personal-drive[.]example, 22:47 to 22:52 UTC.

Only observable technical activity, with a timestamp and a source, survives review. Option A wraps the same fact in an intent label nobody has established; that is speculation, and it becomes discoverable the moment it enters a ticket. Option B records personal circumstances the SOC should never hold: HR-held context reaches the case only through the insider-risk route, never as analyst-collected notes. Option C gets the order wrong: the referral's reference, owner and technical questions are all the SOC needs, and the reason for the referral stays with HR and the insider-program lead. The working example's HR referral scenario shows the full record.

column1:
Subject hands its entity map to Scope. Which entities belong on it?

A. Only the entity named in the alert. The map is a pointer, and Scope rebuilds the rest from it.
B. Every entity with a suspicious finding. Cleared entities are dropped to keep the map actionable.
C. Every ring (primary, secondary, downstream), each with its assessment, ruled-out ones included.
D. The human identities only. Service accounts and hosts are infrastructure, tracked elsewhere.
column2:
C. Every ring (primary, secondary, downstream), each with its assessment, ruled-out ones included.

The map carries three rings (primary entities directly named or implicated, secondary entities connected through trust paths, and downstream entities the implicated identities can reach), each with its authentication, authorization, behavior, and relationships assessment, plus any originating threat infrastructure (sender, domain, IP) tracked alongside as threat entities, not internal identities. Confidence labels ride alongside, using the shared rubric. And ruled-out entities stay on the map, because examined-and-cleared is a finding (Case C's laptop is one): dropping them invites the next phase to spend depth re-answering a question Subject already closed.

column1:
A confirmed compromise of a system processing payment card data is detected. The technical investigation will take days. What does Scope require the analyst to do about timing?

A. Wait until the technical investigation finishes, so the notification is accurate the first time it goes out.
B. Skip the compliance step during triage; regulatory work begins only if the case escalates to IR.
C. Engage compliance now and commit the suspicion timestamp, so any notification clocks run in parallel.
D. Hold notice until the investigation confirms data actually left; premature notice causes churn for all.
column2:
C. Engage compliance now and commit the suspicion timestamp, so any notification clocks run in parallel.

Card-brand rules, not PCI DSS itself, set the notification deadlines, and they are short and run from reasonable suspicion: Visa requires a report within three calendar days, routed through the acquirer, and American Express requires notice immediately and no later than 72 hours. Each brand sets its own rules and acquirer contracts can be stricter, so the figure that binds you (Mastercard's included) comes from your acquirer agreement. That clock runs from suspicion, not from the end of a days-long investigation, so waiting for accuracy or for proof that data left both miss it. Analysts do not start or stop the clocks; law and contract do. Scope's job is to recognize the obligation, engage compliance, and commit the timestamp so compliance can run the clock in parallel with the technical work. Deferring it until a case reaches IR spends days the clock does not give back.

column1:
An alert looks like a phishing-driven intrusion. The message trace shows the lure arrived five days before the alert fired. Where does Scope set the backward edge of the primary window?

A. At or before the lure's delivery: the window anchors on the earliest related artifact, not the alert.
B. At 72 hours before the alert, the top of the phishing default; delivery timing is Uncover's question.
C. At the start of retention, so nothing the SOC still holds is left unread in an email-driven intrusion.
D. At the first confirmed malicious action, because activity before execution is background noise.
column2:
A. At or before the lure's delivery: the window anchors on the earliest related artifact, not the alert.

The window follows the threat type and the evidence, not the alert time. The 24-to-72-hour default for phishing assumes initial access was recent; when the evidence shows the lure landed five days earlier, the backward edge moves to that artifact, and the worked examples pair the primary window with a longer look at the primary entities (4 weeks in the finance-team case) to rule out earlier staging. Stopping at 72 hours cuts off the delivery and everything between it and the alert. Starting at execution misses the delivery and any reconnaissance. Reading back to the start of retention is the opposite error: a window with no evidence-based edge is a fishing expedition.

column1:
An alert on a build-pipeline service account smells like possible supply-chain compromise. What historical window does Scope set?

A. 1 to 24 hours. Service accounts are high-volume, and a tight window keeps the queries tractable.
B. 24 to 72 hours, the standard intrusion window that fits most confirmed compromises.
C. 3 to 12 months, the insider window, because a pipeline acting maliciously is an insider by definition.
D. 1 to 6 months. The compromise may predate the alert by weeks, and earlier silent activity matters.
column2:
D. 1 to 6 months. The compromise may predate the alert by weeks, and earlier silent activity matters.

The window follows the threat type, not a default. Supply-chain compromises often predate their first alert by weeks or months: the malicious component may have shipped in an update long since deployed. The 1-to-6-month window is bounded by what the SOC actually retains, and if retention falls short, the gap is documented in the Scope output rather than ignored. The insider option borrows the right length of window for the wrong reason: a compromised pipeline is not an insider.

column1:
The Subject phase identified seven identities connected to the alert. How many should be primary in scope?

A. All seven at full depth. Anything less leaves a potentially compromised identity unexamined.
B. Directly involved identities get full depth; trust-path-connected ones get baseline checks.
C. One, the identity named in the alert. The others belong to Uncover if evidence points there.
D. Three, the number one analyst can profile within the Scope phase's time budget.
column2:
B. Directly involved identities get full depth; trust-path-connected ones get baseline checks.

Primary entities are those directly involved in the alert, plus any other credential of the same principal that the compromise could plausibly carry over to (which is why dlin's federated cloud identity is primary in the worked example). Secondary entities are connected through trust paths but not in the alert. The split keeps investigation depth proportional to evidence rather than spending equal time on every identity in the map. A fixed count, high or low, ignores the evidence the split is supposed to follow.

column1:
Alert and Subject both lean benign on a developer-workstation alert, but the user's account can reach a dozen other systems. How does Scope draw the boundary?

A. Narrow: the user, the workstation, the flagged process. Unevidenced systems stay out; the expansion path is written.
B. Wide: add every reachable system as a secondary entity. Broad scope is cheap insurance while the verdict is still open.
C. Split the difference: add the three most sensitive reachable systems as secondaries, and watch only those.
D. Skip the formal boundary: a probable benign close does not need scoping, so go straight to Uncover.
column2:
A. Narrow: the user, the workstation, the flagged process. Unevidenced systems stay out; the expansion path is written.

This is restraint scoping, and it is as much a Scope skill as expansion. Access alone is topology, not evidence, and every entity added spends Uncover's depth where there is no signal. The narrow boundary is defensible precisely because the expansion path exists: if Uncover surfaces evidence touching another system, the decision tree grows the boundary with a documented justification. Restraint is not the same as skipping checks: a bounded check that answers the verdict question, like the extension-layer check in the Cursor case, stays in. Sprawl on a benign-leaning case is how a fast close becomes a five-hour one.

column1:
An investigation needs in-app activity from a SaaS platform, but the SOC only has authentication logs and aggregate API call counts. What does Scope require?

A. Work with what is available; visibility gaps are universal and not worth a line in the record.
B. Pause the investigation until the vendor data arrives, so conclusions rest on full evidence.
C. Reconstruct the in-app activity from authentication patterns, which is close enough for triage.
D. Name the gap explicitly in the Scope output and submit the vendor data request now.
column2:
D. Name the gap explicitly in the Scope output and submit the vendor data request now.

Naming what cannot be seen is part of Scope. It prevents wasted effort on impossible queries, it keeps the record from reading a gap as quiet, and it lets the analyst submit vendor or external-team requests early so the data arrives in parallel. Pausing the case for the vendor stalls everything else the boundary allows Uncover to do.

column1:
A hospital SOC confirms a compromised workstation had access to systems holding PHI. When does HIPAA's 60-day individual-notification clock start?

A. When the technical investigation confirms that PHI actually left the covered entity's own environment.
B. When the privacy officer formally opens a breach case in the compliance system and assigns an owner.
C. At discovery: when any workforce member knew or reasonably should have known, which can be the alert.
D. When counsel signs off on the four-factor risk assessment concluding that a breach occurred.
column2:
C. At discovery: when any workforce member knew or reasonably should have known, which can be the alert.

The 60-day clock (45 CFR §164.404) runs from discovery, not from confirmation; discovery is a knew-or-should-have-known standard applied to the whole workforce. The alert that starts triage can be the discovery event, which is why Scope commits the timestamp and engages the privacy officer early. The four-factor assessment (§164.402) decides whether notification is required at all; it does not pause the clock. Sixty days is the outer limit; the standard is without unreasonable delay.

column1:
During Scope, the analyst confirms that a compromised account assumed a cloud role during the investigation window. The decision-tree response is...

A. Note it but stay focused on the originating endpoint until Uncover produces evidence.
B. Add the role and its reachable resources into scope; review AssumeRole patterns vs. normal.
C. Immediately isolate every system the role can access before the session can be used again.
D. Keep scope as-is until Uncover finds evidence of misuse; expansion without evidence is churn.
column2:
B. Add the role and its reachable resources into scope; review AssumeRole patterns vs. normal.

The IF/THEN decision-tree pattern is Scope's structured way of evolving the boundary. A cloud-role assumption is evidence; the methodology says incorporate it now and document the three-line justification (evidence, risk, required actions) so the expansion is defensible. The role itself gets full depth and the resources it can reach start at baseline, upgraded on any signal. Waiting for Uncover to surface it would mean Uncover queries outside its own scope to find what Scope should have already framed.

column1:
Scope confirms a compromised identity can reach systems inside the cardholder data environment (CDE). What does the methodology require?

A. Request full CDE access for the analyst so that cardholder-data exposure can be sampled directly and fast.
B. Wait for confirmed cardholder-data exfiltration before involving compliance or the acquirer.
C. Isolate every CDE system immediately; PCI DSS requires containment within one hour of detection.
D. Tag it PCI-relevant, request that CDE logs be held, and tell the acquirer-relationship owner today.
column2:
D. Tag it PCI-relevant, request that CDE logs be held, and tell the acquirer-relationship owner today.

Card-brand clocks run from reasonable suspicion, not confirmation (Visa: a report within three calendar days; American Express: no later than 72 hours), and they reach the brands through the acquirer, so the acquirer-relationship owner hears the same day. A PCI Forensic Investigator may later re-examine everything preserved in the first hours. If the environment actually meets PCI DSS v4.0.1 Req. 10.5.1 (at least 12 months of audit-log history, the most recent three months immediately available), that is the minimum look-back to expect, but a requirement is not a guarantee: verify that the CDE logs for the window exist and were not tampered with before relying on them. Identifying what will rotate or be cleaned up before the case can use it, and requesting the retention extension or hold through the owning team, is still the analyst's job. Investigative access into the CDE follows the same least-privilege controls as any other access: defaulting to full access is exactly backwards.

column1:
A US SOC investigates a compromised account belonging to an employee in Germany, with the relevant logs stored in an EU region. What does Scope's sovereignty boundary require?

A. Check transfer and residency limits before moving data; the work may run in-region or via a regional team.
B. Copy the EU logs into the US SIEM. Centralized analysis beats jurisdictional caution during an active incident.
C. Proceed normally. Sovereignty is a legal-team concern that begins only after triage has closed the case.
D. Strip usernames from the logs before transfer; anonymized data is exempt from cross-border transfer rules.
column2:
A. Check transfer and residency limits before moving data; the work may run in-region or via a regional team.

Cross-border rules can restrict moving or even remotely viewing log data. GDPR Chapter V treats access from the US as a transfer that needs a valid mechanism (an adequacy decision or standard contractual clauses), some contracts and national laws impose true residency, and for German staff a works-council agreement may limit what can be examined at all. Scope is where that constraint is recognized, because discovering it mid-Uncover means evidence already moved where it should not have. The anonymize option fails because stripping usernames is pseudonymization, not anonymization: data that can be re-linked to a person remains personal data (GDPR Recital 26), so the constraint still applies.

column1:
Every handoff in the worked example lists open questions for Uncover. Why does Scope include them?

A. Standard format: the documentation templates require an open-questions section in every record.
B. For the audit trail: reviewers check that every open question was eventually answered in full.
C. To point Uncover at the critical unknowns, because specific questions drive specific queries.
D. Because Uncover cannot read Subject's findings and needs the open items restated for it.
column2:
C. To point Uncover at the critical unknowns, because specific questions drive specific queries.

Each open question in the worked example maps to a query Uncover can run. Case C's handoff asks what the session and the app actually read, whether the attacker reached payment threads or the CRM, and whether the tenant sweeps surface other sessions, grants or exposed accounts; Uncover answers each one from the audit log and the sweep. Framing the questions before the data is pulled is what keeps Uncover from running broad queries and hoping. The format and audit options describe side effects, not the purpose, and Uncover reads Subject's findings directly.

column1:
An identity-only case has no host in question: a replayed session, an OAuth consent grant, and a hiding inbox rule, all in a SaaS tenant. What does the infrastructure boundary consist of?

A. The user's laptop and its network segment, because every identity is used from some device.
B. Named log queries over set windows: sessions, grants, rules and mailboxes, plus a tenant sweep.
C. Every SaaS tenant the user can reach, held as downstream until its vendor clears each one.
D. Nothing formal: identity cases have no perimeter, so Uncover follows the session where it leads.
column2:
B. Named log queries over set windows: sessions, grants, rules and mailboxes, plus a tenant sweep.

When the infrastructure is someone else's cloud, the boundary is a query set: which sessions, which grants, which mailboxes, over which windows. Case C writes the tenant sweep (proxy-IP sign-ins, attacker-ASN sessions, same-app consents, same-shape rules, MFA registrations) into the boundary so Uncover runs it once, deliberately. The laptop option scopes the wrong plane: rvega's laptop was examined and cleared. Holding every reachable tenant in scope is topology, not evidence, and 'no perimeter' is how an identity case sprawls.

column1:
Scope wants six months of SaaS audit history for a user, but the platform keeps 90 days. The query for the older period returns no rows. What goes in the record?

A. No activity found for the six-month window, since the query ran cleanly and returned no rows.
B. Nothing yet; a gap only matters if Uncover ends up needing that older period for its verdict.
C. The 90-day result alone, with the window shortened so the boundary matches the data held.
D. A named visibility gap for the dark period, recorded as unknown rather than as no activity.
column2:
D. A named visibility gap for the dark period, recorded as unknown rather than as no activity.

A query against logs that were never kept returns nothing, and nothing looks exactly like a clean result. That is why Scope checks retention before Uncover runs the query. The dark period is a visibility gap: it is named in the boundary statement, it lowers confidence (unknown is not Low), and it is never written up as 'no activity'. Quietly shortening the window hides the gap the record exists to show, and deferring it leaves Uncover and Risk reading silence as evidence.

column1:
A compromised mailbox holds customer personal data, some of it about people in the EU. Nothing is yet known to have left the tenant. When does GDPR's 72-hour authority-notification clock start?

A. At awareness: when the organization has a reasonable degree of certainty that personal data was compromised.
B. When the investigation confirms exfiltration; with no data leaving the tenant there is no breach to report.
C. When the DPO completes the formal risk assessment and signs off that a notifiable breach has in fact occurred.
D. When IR closes the incident, so the authority receives a full and accurate account the first time.
column2:
A. At awareness: when the organization has a reasonable degree of certainty that personal data was compromised.

Article 33's clock runs from awareness, which the EDPB describes as a reasonable degree of certainty that a security incident has compromised personal data. Unauthorized access is a breach of confidentiality even if nothing left, so 'no exfiltration, no breach' is wrong. The DPO's assessment decides whether to notify, and it has to happen inside the 72 hours, not before they start. In the worked example, Scope records 09:22 as the candidate awareness timestamp in the token-theft case for exactly this reason.

column1:
At a US public company, a cyber incident may be material. When is the Form 8-K Item 1.05 disclosure due?

A. Within four business days of the SOC first discovering the incident, whatever its materiality turns out to be.
B. Within 72 hours of the first alert, matching the GDPR clock that most privacy programs already track.
C. Within four business days of the materiality determination, which must be made without unreasonable delay.
D. Only once the investigation is complete, so that the filing describes the full impact accurately.
column2:
C. Within four business days of the materiality determination, which must be made without unreasonable delay.

Item 1.05 runs from the company's determination that the incident is material, and that determination must itself be made without unreasonable delay after discovery. Disclosure counsel and executives make the materiality call, but they make it from the case record: scope of access, data classes, business functions affected. Vague or missing facts slow a determination the SEC expects promptly, which is why Scope commits them early rather than waiting for the investigation to finish.

column1:
A breach exposes personal information of California residents. Under California's breach-notification law as amended effective 1 January 2026, when must residents be notified?

A. In the most expedient time possible, with no fixed deadline, once the investigation is complete.
B. Within 30 calendar days of discovery, with delay only for law enforcement or to scope and restore.
C. Within 72 hours of awareness, mirroring GDPR, with the Attorney General notified at the same time.
D. Within 60 days of discovery, the same outer limit that HIPAA sets for individual breach notification.
column2:
B. Within 30 calendar days of discovery, with delay only for law enforcement or to scope and restore.

SB 446 amended Cal. Civ. Code §1798.82, effective 1 January 2026: residents must be notified within 30 calendar days of discovery, and delay is allowed only at law enforcement's request or as needed to determine the breach's scope and restore the system's integrity. When more than 500 residents are notified, a sample notice goes to the Attorney General within 15 days of notifying them. The older 'most expedient time possible' wording, with no fixed clock, is out of date. Scope's contribution is the same as for every regime: the discovery timestamp and the categories of personal information in reach.

column1:
Your company hosts a customer's personal data as their processor. Scope finds that an attacker plausibly read some of it. What does GDPR Article 33 expect from your side?

A. Notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours yourselves, because the breach happened on your systems.
B. Nothing until the customer asks; as a processor, breach notification is wholly the controller's business.
C. Tell the controller without undue delay; their 72 hours generally start from your notice to them.
D. Wait until exfiltration is confirmed, then send the customer one complete and accurate breach report.
column2:
C. Tell the controller without undue delay; their 72 hours generally start from your notice to them.

Article 33(2) gives a processor one duty: notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of the breach. The controller is generally treated as aware once its processor tells it, so its 72 hours start from your notice, and every hour your side sits on the finding comes out of the customer's window. Many data-processing agreements set a shorter contractual deadline that runs from your discovery. Notifying the authority is the controller's call (Art. 33(1)), not yours. Waiting for exfiltration repeats the confirmation error: unauthorized access is already a breach of confidentiality. Scope's part is the same as always: commit the timestamp, and get the privacy owner who holds the agreement into the case.

column1:
A threat intel feed says a particular domain is associated with a known campaign. The analyst sees the same domain in firewall logs from one host. What is the right next step?

A. Treat the match as a hypothesis: check which process connected and whether the pattern fits.
B. Block the domain at the perimeter now; a campaign association is action-worthy on its own.
C. Escalate to IR now; a campaign domain in local firewall logs meets the confirmed-malicious bar.
D. Ignore it. Campaign domains rotate too fast for a feed match to mean anything in local logs.
column2:
A. Treat the match as a hypothesis: check which process connected and whether the pattern fits.

Threat intelligence is most useful as a hypothesis. The matched domain is a starting point, not a verdict. Validate against the actual telemetry (which process, which user, which pattern) before acting. Escalating on the match alone skips that step: confirmed means high confidence on the shared rubric, and a single feed association is a lead that refines Scope, not a page to IR.

column1:
A dropper hash matches a known campaign's tooling, and nothing else links the case to that actor. What confidence label can attribution carry in the case file?

A. HIGH. A hash match is exact by definition, and hashes do not collide in practice.
B. MEDIUM. One solid technical indicator sits squarely in the middle of the scale.
C. None. Attribution is not a triage activity, so it does not belong in the case file.
D. LOW. One indicator in one category; shared tooling makes coincidence plausible.
column2:
D. LOW. One indicator in one category; shared tooling makes coincidence plausible.

One indicator in one category is LOW, and the reason is not hash collisions: shared, sold, and leaked tooling means the same dropper turns up in unrelated hands, so the overlap can be coincidental even though the match is exact. What lifts the label is correlation across diverse categories: if the C2 infrastructure and the TTP chain also match the same campaign, the claim earns MEDIUM. Attribution stays in the case file at its honest label, because promoting low-confidence attribution into operational decisions is a common and costly attribution failure.

column1:
Which layer of adversary behavior can attackers change most cheaply without changing their goal: tactics, techniques, or procedures?

A. Tactics
B. Procedures
C. Techniques
D. All three change at about the same rate.
column2:
B. Procedures

Procedures (specific implementations) change rapidly as adversaries adapt their tooling. Techniques (the methods) change more slowly. Tactics (the goals) are nearly stable over years. The broader point, that behavior-based detection outlasts indicator matching, is David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain, which puts TTPs as a whole at the top.

column1:
An investigation needs to know whether a file was executed on an endpoint earlier this week. Which data source answers this most directly?

A. SIEM
B. FIM
C. EDR
D. Network analysis
column2:
C. EDR

EDR captures process creation events that show whether a file was executed, and a few days is comfortably inside a typical retention window. FIM tells you the file exists or was modified, but not whether it ran. SIEM aggregates from other sources. One caveat worth knowing: for questions like did this ever run, beyond the EDR retention window, the answer lives in whatever long-term store (SIEM or data lake) archives the EDR telemetry.

column1:
An investigation needs both an EDR process timeline and a SIEM-wide authentication search. The SIEM search's accounts and time window depend on what the EDR timeline shows. Which query runs first?

A. The SIEM search. It covers everything, so it can only shrink the work the EDR query has to do.
B. Both at once. Serializing queries wastes wall-clock time in a phase measured in minutes.
C. Whichever tool is already open. Query order does not change the evidence that comes back.
D. The EDR query. The cheapest, most specific query runs first and narrows the broad one.
column2:
D. The EDR query. The cheapest, most specific query runs first and narrows the broad one.

The tooling pattern is cheapest or most specific first. The EDR query is scoped to one host and returns fast, and its result narrows the time window and the entities, which turns the SIEM search from an everything-scan into a targeted pull. Running both at once sounds efficient, but the broad query's parameters depend on the narrow query's result: launched unanchored, the SIEM search returns a haystack that costs more analyst time than the parallelism saved.

column1:
A firewall session at 10:04:12 and an EDR process start at 10:04:13 sit on the same host, and the verdict depends on which came first. Neither source's clock has been verified. What do you do?

A. Order them as logged: the EDR event is a second later, so the process followed the connection.
B. Treat them as unordered and find evidence that settles the sequence without the clocks.
C. Trust the EDR clock, since endpoint agents sync time more reliably than network appliances.
D. Average the two timestamps and record the midpoint as the time of one combined event.
column2:
B. Treat them as unordered and find evidence that settles the sequence without the clocks.

Two events from different sources a second apart are simultaneous for reasoning purposes unless both clocks are verified. If a conclusion depends on order inside the skew window, the conclusion needs different evidence: a parent-child relationship, a source port that ties the connection to the process, or a third source with a verified clock. Picking a spine clock tells you which timeline to hang events on; it does not make an unverified one-second gap meaningful.

column1:
A fleet query for the C2 domain returns zero rows outside the first host. Before you record 'other hosts contacted the domain' as refuted, what must you confirm?

A. Nothing more. Zero rows from a fleet-wide query is the negative result the ledger needs.
B. That a second analyst reran the same query and got the same zero rows on their own.
C. That the query finds rows for a known-visited domain and the source covers every host.
D. That threat intel lists no other victims of this campaign in your industry this quarter.
column2:
C. That the query finds rows for a known-visited domain and the source covers every host.

An empty result only counts as evidence of absence when the query could have found something. A control query (the same query against a domain you know hosts visited) proves the field names and syntax work, and coverage (sensor and log-source health, onboarding, retention, and hosts that bypass the proxy) proves the source could see the hosts in question. Rerunning the same query repeats the same blind spot. Two empty pivots plus the four dry-thread checks is a defensible stop.

column1:
Sorted by _indextime, the SIEM puts a Wednesday event ahead of a Tuesday event from the same host. What is the most likely explanation?

A. The SIEM is sorting by arrival time; a forwarder delivered the Tuesday event late.
B. The host's clock was wrong on Tuesday, so the event really belongs on Wednesday.
C. An attacker edited the Tuesday log entry so that it looks earlier than it really was.
D. Index time is event time for SIEM purposes, so the Wednesday event really came first.
column2:
A. The SIEM is sorting by arrival time; a forwarder delivered the Tuesday event late.

_indextime records when the event arrived, and forwarders batch, retry, and fall behind, so arrival order is not event order. Sort on event time (_time in Splunk, TimeGenerated in Sentinel, @timestamp in Elastic) and check that the parser filled it: if event time equals ingest time on every row, the parser failed. Clock error and tampering are possible, but they are hypotheses to test after the cheap explanation is ruled out.

column1:
A suspected intrusion may have started six weeks ago, but the SOC's EDR retains 14 days of telemetry. Which data-source principle is at stake?

A. Historical depth: days of retention cannot say whether this began before the alert.
B. Comprehensive coverage: some endpoint classes in the fleet have no EDR sensor at all.
C. Contextual analysis: EDR alone cannot tell the story without identity and network logs.
D. Data integrity: telemetry past its retention window no longer holds up as evidence.
column2:
A. Historical depth: days of retention cannot say whether this began before the alert.

Retention shapes what is even possible to investigate. Sophisticated intrusions unfold over weeks or months, and a source holding 14 days cannot answer 'did this start before the alert?' no matter how well the query is written. The practical moves are knowing where the longer archive lives (the SIEM or data lake that retains the EDR feed) and, where none does, recording the unanswerable window as a gap (temporal depth, not layer coverage) instead of treating silence as evidence of absence.

column1:
Why should the Uncover narrative carry ATT&CK technique tags?

A. Tags make the record shorter, and shorter records are what downstream readers finish.
B. Most compliance frameworks require ATT&CK mappings in escalated-incident records.
C. They are a shared vocabulary IR, detection engineering, and trend analysis all read.
D. Tags can replace the narrative, which is slower to write and harder to read under pressure.
column2:
C. They are a shared vocabulary IR, detection engineering, and trend analysis all read.

ATT&CK tags turn analyst observations into a portable artifact. The same techniques mean something to the IR responder, the detection engineer who decides what to tune, and the leader tracking threat trends over time. The tags make the narrative portable; they do not replace it, because ATT&CK is an unordered taxonomy and the sequence is the analyst's contribution. Cases with no adversary behavior record 'none observed' rather than forcing a mapping.

column1:
An XDR console presents one incident that stitches together an email alert, an endpoint alert, and an identity alert. What do you check before treating it as one case?

A. Nothing. The vendor's correlation engine is tuned on far more data than any one SOC sees.
B. The join keys behind the stitch: a shared host, account, or session in a stated window.
C. The severity score. A high combined severity confirms the three alerts belong together.
D. Whether all three alerts came from one vendor, which guarantees consistent timestamps.
column2:
B. The join keys behind the stitch: a shared host, account, or session in a stated window.

XDR automates the join, not the judgment. Before inheriting the stitch, check what joined the alerts: a shared host ID, account, session ID, or message ID inside a plausible window is a real join; a shared IP behind NAT or a loose time window is coincidence-prone. Grouped alerts form one case whose riskiest member sets its level, so a wrong stitch both inflates work and hides it.

column1:
An analyst is investigating a possible compromise on a macOS developer workstation. The user's role legitimately involves scripting, IDE plugin processes, and encrypted outbound traffic. What does the methodology require Uncover to produce if the evidence supports a benign verdict?

A. Nothing beyond the closure itself. A benign verdict ends the Uncover obligation.
B. A one-line entry, 'benign, developer tooling', in the case notes before closing.
C. An escalation anyway; surface-suspicious activity needs an IR review before any close.
D. The same rigor as a positive finding: evidence chain, confidence, gaps, and feedback.
column2:
D. The same rigor as a positive finding: evidence chain, confidence, gaps, and feedback.

A benign verdict that meets the methodology's standard is not dismissed. It is documented, evidenced, and bounded, including which axis cleared it: here the rule detected exactly the behavior it describes (detection: true positive) and the activity was authorized, a benign true positive. That documentation is what lets the case re-open with full context if new signals appear, and what lets the next identical fire close against a written pattern entry instead of starting from zero.

column1:
Risk receives an Uncover handoff. Which of these is Risk's job?

A. Rate impact, likelihood and confidence; recommend close, escalate, or rescope.
B. Isolate the compromised host before the adversary can react to the detection.
C. Start regulator notification once the evidence shows regulated data was touched.
D. Tune the detection rule that fired so the same alert stops consuming the queue.
column2:
A. Rate impact, likelihood and confidence; recommend close, escalate, or rescope.

Risk is the analytical checkpoint, not the response phase. It rates impact, likelihood, and confidence, places the case in a matrix cell with a priority, and recommends a move: close, escalate, or push back to Scope. Risk recommends; it does not act or decide, and the Escalation decision makes and records the close-or-escalate call. Containment runs there (preservation and pre-authorized actions, then IR). Regulatory notification is not Risk's call either: privacy and legal own it, engaged at Scope when regulated data was flagged, on a clock that runs in parallel with the technical work rather than waiting for Risk. Detection tuning flows from Documentation.

column1:
EDR records powershell.exe (PID 5208) opening an outbound connection at 14:22:31Z. The proxy logs a TLS session from the same host to a newly registered domain at 14:22:31Z. What makes treating these as one event defensible?

A. The identical timestamp. Two independent sources agreeing to the second is the correlation.
B. The domain's age. A newly registered destination pulls any nearby telemetry into the case.
C. The join keys agree: same host, same second, same connection (destination or client port).
D. Nothing extra. Once EDR ties the connection to a process, the proxy record adds nothing.
column2:
C. The join keys agree: same host, same second, same connection (destination or client port).

Correlation is defensible when independent sources agree on the keys that identify the event: the host, the time, and the connection. A timestamp alone can collide and hosts make many simultaneous connections. The proxy adds what EDR usually cannot see: the requested hostname (from the CONNECT line or the TLS SNI), TLS metadata, and bytes transferred, plus the full URI only where the proxy decrypts TLS. Behind an explicit proxy, EDR records the proxy's own address as the destination, so the join becomes host, time, and client source port (where the proxy logs it). The worked example does exactly this: the proxy session matching the EDR network event on host, client source port, and time is what turns two log lines into one attributed action. The source port only joins cleanly where nothing translates addresses between the host and the log source; behind NAT, match on the translated tuple or fall back to host, time, and destination.

column1:
GuardDuty raises Exfiltration:S3/AnomalousBehavior on a 02:14 UTC session: an engineer assumed a role documented as automation-only (CI), with read access to a regulated bucket. CloudTrail shows eight reads of quarterly-export files, no ListObjects reconnaissance, no writes, corporate VPN egress throughout. The IdP shows a FIDO2 login from the registered device with no token-replay or consent-grant indicators. What does Uncover conclude?

A. Compromise confirmed: an off-hours human assumption of a CI role on regulated data is conclusive.
B. Confirmed control violation, intent unresolved; only independent authorization evidence closes it.
C. Likely a benign export: the engineer's confirmation plus the clean identity surface closes it.
D. No verdict yet: without a forensic image of the laptop, the cloud logs cannot support one either way.
column2:
B. Confirmed control violation, intent unresolved; only independent authorization evidence closes it.

The clean identity surface does real work: it makes token theft, consent-grant abuse, and AiTM phishing less likely, because each would leave marks that are absent. But it answers who authenticated, not who authorized. A human interactively using a role documented as automation-only against regulated data is a policy violation in every branch, including the friendly one, and a fresh STS session is still a replayable credential while it lives. The engineer's own confirmation would be a lead, not closure; what closes the case is an approved work item verified with its owner, the data owner's authorization, and evidence of where the exported files went after download (the destination CloudTrail cannot show). Compromise-confirmed overclaims the same evidence in the other direction, and waiting for a full forensic image of the laptop overcorrects: the cloud logs already support the violation verdict, and device-level evidence is a closing item, not a precondition.

column1:
The case needs to answer one question before Risk: did data actually leave the environment? Which evidence combination answers it?

A. EDR alone. Process telemetry shows file reads and network sends from one process tree.
B. Threat intelligence. If the actor's campaigns exfiltrate, treat exfiltration as established.
C. The vulnerability scanner, which shows whether an exfiltration-capable exposure existed.
D. Telemetry where the data crosses an observable boundary, aligned to the endpoint timeline.
column2:
D. Telemetry where the data crosses an observable boundary, aligned to the endpoint timeline.

Exfiltration is proven where the data crosses a boundary you can observe: network egress (proxy, firewall, DLP) for network paths, the provider's audit and data-access logs for cloud and SaaS paths, and endpoint DLP or device-control logs for removable media. EDR alone shows that a process read files and sent bytes; volume, destination, and content classification usually live at that crossing point. Aligning those against the endpoint timeline is what turns 'the process could have exfiltrated' into 'this much data moved to this destination at this time', or into a documented negative finding.

column1:
An IDS alert fires for an exploitation attempt against a CVE scored 9.8 under CVSS v3.1, aimed at an internal server. The server runs a patched version, and EDR shows no new processes or callbacks. What should drive the Risk assessment?

A. Whether exploitation succeeded on this target; here it did not, so it scores Low.
B. The 9.8 base score, because a critical score is a reason to escalate on its own.
C. Whether the CVE is in the KEV catalog, since a KEV listing makes the case P1.
D. Whatever the compliance framework for this server prescribes for critical findings.
column2:
A. Whether exploitation succeeded on this target; here it did not, so it scores Low.

CVSS scores the severity of a vulnerability, not an alert, and FIRST says it should not be used alone to assess risk. For an alert that names a CVE, ask whether the target is affected, whether the surface is exposed, whether the CVE is in KEV or high on EPSS, and above all whether exploitation succeeded. A patched target and no follow-on activity make this an attempt, scored Low on exploitation and scope whatever the base score. KEV and EPSS set how fast the patch or block elsewhere should follow; they do not set this case's band.

column1:
Impact and likelihood are...

A. Two ways of measuring the same underlying severity from different directions.
B. Judgment calls where a senior analyst's intuition outperforms an explicit rubric.
C. Independent dimensions, evaluated separately and then deliberately combined.
D. Two factors that must be multiplied into a single numeric score for the record.
column2:
C. Independent dimensions, evaluated separately and then deliberately combined.

Impact is 'if this is real, how bad is it.' Likelihood is 'how probable is it that this activity is malicious,' with the analyst's confidence in that estimate recorded beside it. Separating them prevents the common error of letting impact bias the likelihood judgment.

column1:
A case closes benign: the rule fired correctly on an authorized admin script. What should the analyst record?

A. Nothing beyond the closure code. A benign close is a non-event by definition.
B. Both verdict axes, what was checked, what ruled malice out, and the follow-up.
C. A one-line summary, enough to show the alert was reviewed before it closed.
D. A tuning request to detection engineering, since the rule fired on benign activity.
column2:
B. Both verdict axes, what was checked, what ruled malice out, and the follow-up.

A benign close is a finding too. Record the verdict on both axes (here: detection true positive; activity authorized, a benign true positive), what was checked, what ruled malice out, and what the close should change. Because the rule read the activity correctly, the follow-up is context-side (document it, or a pattern entry if it recurs), not a tuning request: writing 'false positive' here would invite de-tuning a rule that works.

column1:
Risk's written assessment for a case should include...

A. A single composite number, so assessments can be compared and trended across cases.
B. The matrix cell alone; the scoring detail behind it stays in the analyst's own working notes.
C. A verbal recommendation to the SOC manager, who owns the written record of the case.
D. Impact, likelihood, confidence, the cell and band, open questions, and a recommended move.
column2:
D. Impact, likelihood, confidence, the cell and band, open questions, and a recommended move.

The Risk output should be a one-page record that a future reviewer can read and understand without re-doing the analysis: impact and likelihood justified separately, confidence on the shared rubric, the cell and its band (plus any override that fired), open questions, and a recommended move. Risk recommends; the Escalation decision decides and records the call.

column1:
The RATM rubric scores a case as High asset criticality (crown-jewel database). The only malicious indicator is a signature match; the host's EDR telemetry is complete for the window and shows no execution or follow-on behavior. The matrix reads High impact / Low likelihood. What is the default action?

A. Keep working on the high-impact clock; raise priority if evidence strengthens.
B. Escalate immediately, because a crown-jewel database is at stake in this particular case.
C. Standard queue, because a Low likelihood always means a low-priority case.
D. Close as a false positive, because signatures without behavior are only noise.
column2:
A. Keep working on the high-impact clock; raise priority if evidence strengthens.

Impact answers what is at stake if the finding is real; likelihood answers how probable it is that the activity is malicious. High impact with examined, benign-leaning evidence is neither an escalation (that would let the stakes inflate the estimate) nor a closure (that would let a quiet signature excuse a crown-jewel case). Two qualifiers from the override rules. This Low is legitimate because the telemetry was present and examined. If likelihood were 'low' because telemetry was missing, unknown is not Low: likelihood reads Medium with confidence Low, the cell becomes High/Medium, and the case is P2, escalate within 4 hours. And a High-impact P3 runs the tightened clock: re-score within 4 hours by default, not 24, with the queue lead aware.

column1:
Uncover confirms the adversary has reached a system outside the original Scope boundary. What does the methodology require?

A. Note the finding for the record but keep working the case inside its original Scope boundary.
B. Loop back through Scope, Uncover, and Risk with the refined boundary before deciding.
C. Escalate now (confirmed spread is a canonical criterion) and keep the loop running for IR.
D. Close this case and open a fresh one scoped to the newly discovered system from the start.
column2:
C. Escalate now (confirmed spread is a canonical criterion) and keep the loop running for IR.

Confirmed lateral movement beyond the boundary meets a canonical escalation criterion, and the escalation tripwire fires from any phase the moment a criterion is confirmed (High on the shared confidence rubric). The dynamic loop still runs (refining scope is exactly what IR needs next), but it runs in parallel with containment, as tasks the IR owner assigns, not instead of it. The loop is for building fidelity on unresolved cases; it is never a reason to sit on a confirmed, spreading compromise.

column1:
A SOC sees the same alert fire repeatedly across multiple developer workstations, and every investigation closes benign. What is the right response?

A. Keep closing them one at a time with full records, since each case stands on its own evidence.
B. Treat the pattern as detection feedback: a role-aware rule variant or a scoped, expiring suppression.
C. Suppress the rule entirely, since a rule this noisy costs far more attention than it could ever return.
D. Escalate the volume to leadership so the detection budget conversation happens further upstream.
column2:
B. Treat the pattern as detection feedback: a role-aware rule variant or a scoped, expiring suppression.

A single benign fire is a closure with feedback. A pattern of benign fires on the same asset class, whether false positives or benign true positives, is a signal about the detection stack itself. The methodology asks for a refined variant or a documented suppression keyed to the tool version, extension or plugin ID, and destination set, with an owner, an expiry and re-fire triggers; never one keyed to signer and install path alone, and never individual repeat closures or wholesale rule removal.

column1:
The Risk assessment for the Cursor IDE case (benign true positive) reads 'High impact, Low likelihood, High confidence: P3; documented close recommended if the forward watch stays clean.' What value does the documented closure provide?

A. A defensible record, detection feedback, a coverage-gap question, and re-openable context.
B. None. A benign close that never escalated produced nothing the wider organization can use.
C. An audit checkbox: evidence the queue is worked, with no investigative value beyond that.
D. A throughput metric: closed cases are how triage capacity gets measured and staffed.
column2:
A. A defensible record, detection feedback, a coverage-gap question, and re-openable context.

A documented benign closure is not a non-event. It is the artifact that defends the case if the same alert fires again, surfaces detection-engineering feedback, raises program-level questions (here, whether TLS-metadata-only visibility to AI-tool vendor endpoints and the lack of USB device control are acceptable), and provides full context if the case needs to re-open. Clarity, not escalation, is the primary outcome of effective triage.

column1:
Two vulnerabilities sit on comparable internet-facing production web servers. Vuln A: CVSS v3.1 9.8, not in CISA's KEV catalog, EPSS 0.01. Vuln B: CVSS v3.1 7.5, listed in KEV, EPSS 0.92. Which drives today's urgency, and why?

A. Vuln A, because its higher base score means worse damage if it is ever exploited.
B. Both equally, because both base scores sit in bands that call for the same clock.
C. Neither, until an alert shows exploitation; vulnerability data has no place in triage.
D. Vuln B: KEV confirms active exploitation, and EPSS rates near-term use as likely.
column2:
D. Vuln B: KEV confirms active exploitation, and EPSS rates near-term use as likely.

KEV confirms the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, and EPSS estimates a high probability of exploitation in the next 30 days; together they outweigh A's higher base severity. As the framework page puts it, a 9.8 nobody exploits matters less today than a 7.2 being actively used. The reverse does not hold, though: absence from KEV is not evidence of safety, and EPSS knows nothing about your exposure or controls, so A still gets patched on its own clock.

column1:
An adversary-in-the-middle phish gave an attacker a user's live session, and an OAuth app consented from that session now reads her mailbox. Evidence is preserved. Which first step actually cuts the attacker's access?

A. Reset her password and re-enroll MFA, since a new password ends every attacker session.
B. Wait for the vendor's item-level read logs, so containment matches the confirmed scope.
C. Revoke her sessions and refresh tokens, disable the app's sign-in, then verify both.
D. Block the phishing domain at the proxy, so no more credentials can be relayed through it.
column2:
