C. Revoke her sessions and refresh tokens, disable the app's sign-in, then verify both.

A password reset may or may not end existing sessions, depending on the identity provider and how the reset is done, and it never removes an app's consent grant. Explicit revocation is the version you can verify: revoke sessions and refresh tokens, disable the app's sign-in, then confirm the attacker's session stops presenting. Those steps are reversible, so they sit on the pre-authorized list; removing the grant and resetting the password follow with IR's approval. Blocking the domain protects the next user, not this one, and waiting for logs leaves live access open.

column1:
A sanctioned vulnerability scanner trips a port-scan rule every week, doing exactly what the rule describes. What are the verdict and the right fix?

A. A false positive; tune the rule so port scans from internal ranges stop firing it.
B. A benign true positive; a pattern entry or scoped exception with owner and expiry.
C. A false positive; disable the rule, since the scanner is all it ever catches.
D. A benign true positive; no record is needed, because nothing malicious happened.
column2:
B. A benign true positive; a pattern entry or scoped exception with owner and expiry.

The rule read the activity correctly and the activity was authorized: a benign true positive. Its fix is context-side, scoped to the scanner (its hosts, schedule, and target set), with an owner, an expiry, and re-fire triggers, and the rule stays as written so it still catches an unsanctioned scan. Calling it a false positive invites de-tuning a rule that works, and every close, benign or not, still gets a record.

column1:
Mid-investigation, the evidence confirms one canonical escalation criterion, but the analyst feels the case would be stronger after finishing the remaining phases. What should they do?

A. Escalate now. One confirmed criterion is the pre-committed answer; the packet finishes in parallel.
B. Finish the remaining phases first; a complete packet is what makes the handoff survive a cold read later.
C. Ask the SOC manager whether this particular case is worth the noise of an escalation.
D. Downgrade the case and keep investigating; escalating on one criterion invites alert fatigue.
column2:
A. Escalate now. One confirmed criterion is the pre-committed answer; the packet finishes in parallel.

Pre-defined criteria exist precisely to remove this judgment call under pressure. One confirmed criterion escalates the case from whatever phase the investigation is in: that is the escalation tripwire, and the packet finishes in parallel. A confirmed criterion is not overridable by the triage analyst. If the analyst disagrees, the disagreement goes into the packet with its evidence, and only the receiving owner can hand the case back or de-escalate it, with a named reason.

column1:
What is the difference between event triage and incident response?

A. Scale: triage handles single-host cases, and IR takes over once multiple systems are involved.
B. Seniority: triage is the analyst queue, and IR is where the senior responders on the bench sit.
C. Sequence: they are the same investigative work, split into before and after the P1 page goes out.
D. The question: triage asks whether it is real and needs more than triage; IR asks how to stop it.
column2:
D. The question: triage asks whether it is real and needs more than triage; IR asks how to stop it.

The distinction is about the question being asked. Triage asks 'is this real, and does it need more than triage?' IR asks 'how do we stop it?' Different outputs follow: a closure record or a handoff packet from triage; containment, eradication, and recovery from IR. Conflating them leads to premature escalation or stalled investigations.

column1:
The handoff packet should be optimized for...

A. Brevity. A responder in an active incident reads one page; anything longer goes unread.
B. Letting the next analyst start where this one stopped, without re-asking anything.
C. Compliance reporting, since the packet becomes the regulatory record of the incident.
D. The SOC manager's review, which is the approval gate the escalation must clear first.
column2:
B. Letting the next analyst start where this one stopped, without re-asking anything.

The packet is the bridge between triage and IR. The metric is continuity: whether the next tier can act without asking the triage analyst to re-explain. That takes complete sections and a short opening (the five-minute read); optimizing for brevity or completeness alone fails.

column1:
A handoff packet has all nine sections filled in. What does the methodology still require before it is declared ready?

A. Manager sign-off, a spell-check pass, and a priority re-score against the current queue.
B. Peer review, then compliance review, then legal review, in that order, each one signed off.
C. Three tests: readable in five minutes, names the next decision, survives an uninvolved reader.
D. Nothing. Nine completed sections is the definition of ready; extra gates only delay the handoff.
column2:
C. Three tests: readable in five minutes, names the next decision, survives an uninvolved reader.

Completeness is structural; actionability is functional, and a complete packet can still fail it. The case summary plus Risk verdict should orient the receiving tier in under five minutes. The packet should tee up the specific decision the next tier must make ('isolate the second host', 'engage compliance'), not just describe the case. And an analyst with no prior context should be able to continue the work without the author in the room. The practical check for that last test: hand the packet to an uninvolved peer, and if they cannot state the verdict in one sentence after five minutes, it is not done. On a P1, the receiving responder is the cold reader: page first, and treat their first questions as the test results.

column1:
In the three-tier SOC model, where is the decision usually made that a case becomes a declared incident?

A. Tier 2, where escalated cases get deep technical investigation and containment planning.
B. Tier 1, since it owns the initial true-positive versus false-positive verdict on every alert.
C. Tier 3, since declaring an incident mobilizes legal, communications, and executives.
D. No tier. Declaration is automatic the moment any escalation criterion is met.
column2:
A. Tier 2, where escalated cases get deep technical investigation and containment planning.

Tier 1 receives and validates alerts, closes false positives with detection feedback, and works the case through the ASSURED phases until either a closure is defensible or an escalation criterion is confirmed; meeting a criterion moves the case up, but that is escalation, not declaration. Tier 2 picks up escalated cases for deeper investigation and containment planning and, in this model, holds the decision on whether the case becomes a declared incident (real organizations vary: an IR lead, incident manager, or SOC manager may own it). Tier 3 is the senior technical bench for the cases Tier 2 cannot close; the cross-functional response (incident command, legal, communications, executives) is a separate function that activates once an incident is declared, not a tier. The bar for 'escalate' and the bar for 'declared incident' are different, and keeping them separate is what the tier boundaries encode.

column1:
At 03:10 you confirm an attacker session on a finance user's account. The P1 page to the IR on-call has gone unacknowledged for 15 minutes. What do you do now?

A. Wait for IR to acknowledge; containment of any kind is IR's call, and acting alone forks the record.
B. Segment the finance VLAN and rotate credentials fleet-wide right away; the attacker may already be spreading.
C. Reset the user's password and remove every app consent; those are the fastest ways to cut access.
D. Preserve, take the pre-authorized reversible actions, and page the fallback: the secondary on-call.
column2:
D. Preserve, take the pre-authorized reversible actions, and page the fallback: the secondary on-call.

The page fell through: at 15 minutes with no acknowledgment, a P1 goes to the secondary on-call, then the SOC manager. Meanwhile the pre-authorized immediate actions exist for exactly this window: preserve the records containment would destroy, then disable the account, revoke its sessions, and disable any consented app's sign-in, all reversible and logged. A password reset and grant removal cannot be undone, so they wait for IR or owner approval; segmenting a network or rotating credentials fleet-wide is containment strategy, and that is IR's call. Waiting does nothing while a confirmed attacker holds a live session.

column1:
The terms 'event', 'alert', and 'incident' get used interchangeably in casual conversation. How does ASSURED distinguish them?

A. They are synonyms in practice; mature SOCs standardize on whichever term the tooling uses.
B. Events are neutral observations; alerts warrant investigation; incidents are actual or imminent violations.
C. Magnitude: an event is small, an alert is medium, and an incident is organization-scale.
D. Source: events come from log pipelines, alerts come from the SIEM, and incidents come from the ticketing system.
column2:
B. Events are neutral observations; alerts warrant investigation; incidents are actual or imminent violations.

ASSURED treats them as distinct concepts with distinct operational meaning. Events are raw observability data. Alerts cross a threshold and become SOC work. An incident, in NIST SP 800-61r3 (2025), adopting the FISMA 2014 definition, is an occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes, without lawful authority, the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of information or an information system, or that violates or imminently threatens to violate law, security policies, security procedures, or acceptable use policies; it is typically confirmed out of one or more alerts and requires coordinated response. Conflating them loses precision under pressure.

column1:
A domain-controller alert fires. Nothing is validated yet, and the domain controller's security log is not reaching the SIEM. What priority does the case get?

A. P1: page IR now. A domain controller is a crown jewel, so any alert on it meets a criterion.
B. P3 on the standard 24-hour clock, since nothing malicious has been confirmed on that host so far.
C. P2: High impact, and missing evidence reads as Medium likelihood, so escalate within 4 hours.
D. Close it as unverifiable; without the security log there is no evidence to triage at all.
column2:
C. P2: High impact, and missing evidence reads as Medium likelihood, so escalate within 4 hours.

Asset value alone is never a confirmed criterion, so this is not the escalation tripwire and not P1 on asset profile. But unknown is not Low: likelihood reads Medium because the evidence is missing, not because it leans benign. High impact with Medium likelihood is the High/Medium cell: P2, acknowledged within 15 minutes and escalated within 4 hours with a complete packet (default clocks; adopters tune them). P3 would apply only if the evidence had been examined and leaned benign, and then on the high-impact clock, not the standard 24 hours. Closing as unverifiable mistakes a telemetry gap for a verdict; the missing log is itself a finding for the packet.

column1:
Risk scores a suspicious-binary case High/Low (P3), and the named re-score trigger comes back clean. What does the Escalation decision produce?

A. Nothing. Escalation only runs when a case escalates; a benign verdict skips the phase.
B. A one-line closure note. Documented rigor is reserved for the cases that go to IR.
C. A courtesy IR review, because a human responder should double-check any close on a pattern-match alert.
D. A close-at-triage record held to handoff rigor: closure check run, targeted notices, full record.
column2:
D. A close-at-triage record held to handoff rigor: closure check run, targeted notices, full record.

Escalation still runs; the decision is a documented close instead of a transfer. The worked example runs a five-item closure check (no escalation criterion confirmed or open as a suspicion; the P3 re-score trigger clean; no persistence or credential access; extension, MCP, workspace-task and agent-command review clean; gaps bounded with reopen triggers written), each backed by Uncover findings or the re-score. Notifications are quiet and targeted: the SOC manager for visibility and close approval, detection engineering with the alert-enrichment request and pattern-entry proposal, nobody else, because loud notices for a documented benign close train the team to discount future ones. The closure record is the decision header the event report opens with. The close is arguably the harder discipline, since the analyst is asking a future reader to trust the absence of compromise.

column1:
Your handoff packet has eight strong sections, but you noticed during the case that you forgot to log the 14:02 page to your SOC manager. What is the right call?

A. Add it now with the true event time, marked as a late entry with the time it was recorded.
B. Add it with the true event time so the Communication record reads cleanly in order.
C. Mention it verbally during the IR handoff so the responders know, but leave the packet as-is.
D. Amend the packet after IR closes the case, when the audit review actually needs the entry.
column2:
A. Add it now with the true event time, marked as a late entry with the time it was recorded.

The Communication record is the ninth section of the handoff packet for exactly this reason, so the page goes in. But a backfilled entry is marked as a late entry: the true event time, plus the time it was recorded. Silent backfill makes the record look contemporaneous when it is not, which undermines audit integrity the moment someone compares it with the paging system's own log. Verbal handoffs and post-close amendments both lose information.

column1:
An attacker holds a session in your mail tenant. You need to page IR, and to ask the user whether she created an inbox rule this morning. Which channels do you use?

A. Tenant email to IR and to the user, marked urgent; both watch their inbox and it leaves a written record.
B. The corporate chat workspace: it is faster than email, and the attacker's foothold is in mail, not chat.
C. Pager and phone bridge for IR; a call to the user on a number from a source the attacker could not edit.
D. Neither for now: hold every contact until IR acknowledges, so nothing tips off the attacker first.
column2:
C. Pager and phone bridge for IR; a call to the user on a number from a source the attacker could not edit.

When a case touches the mail tenant, the chat workspace, or the identity provider that signs users into them, those channels are closed for the case: the adversary may be reading them, and a page or a question sent there lets the attacker watch the response. Chat signs in through the same identity provider, so it is no safer than mail. Page IR by pager and phone bridge, and call the user on a number taken from HR records or a contact list kept outside the affected systems, as it stood before the incident window. Holding every contact is wrong too: the page goes out at once on a trusted channel, and the user's answer can still change the decision before a criterion is confirmed. In Case C, the 09:19 phone call to rvega is what took the case to High confidence.

column1:
A closure record reads 'False positive' for an EDR alert that correctly matched a signed IDE helper, running without its sandbox, launching a child that opened an encrypted connection to the vendor's servers. The activity was authorized. What is wrong with the label?

A. The detection was correct, so this is a benign true positive; record both axes.
B. Nothing. Any alert that did not find malicious activity is a false positive by definition.
C. It should read 'true positive' alone: the rule fired on real behavior, and that is enough.
D. The label is fine, but the record must also open a ticket to suppress the signed helper.
column2:
A. The detection was correct, so this is a benign true positive; record both axes.

The two axes answer different questions. Detection: the rule matched exactly the behavior it describes, so it is a true positive, not a false positive (logic) or (data). Activity: the behavior was authorized, so the verdict is a benign true positive. Calling it a false positive tells detection engineering there is a logic defect to fix when there is none, and hides why the case closed. 'True positive' alone is ambiguous, because many close codes read it as malicious; record both axes.

column1:
A closed record passes every template check: all nine sections are filled and it runs four pages. Each section restates the alert in different words, and nothing in it would help the next analyst work a similar case. Which pitfall is this?

A. Delayed documentation: the record was reconstructed after the case had closed.
B. A sanitization mistake: the record copies detail it never needed to hold.
C. Inconsistent terminology: the sections describe one alert in different words.
D. Form over substance: every field is filled, and none of the reasoning is.
column2:
D. Form over substance: every field is filled, and none of the reasoning is.

Fields filled, value absent: the template was treated as the goal. A short record that carries the reasoning beats a long one that carries none. Nothing in the record suggests it was written late or holds sensitive data, and restating the alert in other words is padding, not terminology drift.

column1:
What is the test of good documentation?

A. Completeness by volume: the longer the record, the more of the case it preserves.
B. A future reader can replay the analyst's reasoning without asking anyone questions.
C. Template fidelity: every section of the standard format is present and filled in.
D. Timeliness: the record was written during the case rather than reconstructed after.
column2:
B. A future reader can replay the analyst's reasoning without asking anyone questions.

The test is whether the record stands alone: a future analyst, auditor, or trainer can read it and understand both what was decided and why. Timeliness is the most important means to that outcome, since a record reconstructed afterwards rarely passes the replay test. Length and template fidelity are neither the test nor a reliable means to it.

column1:
A closed false-positive case is documented. What is its main downstream use?

A. Compliance evidence: proof for auditors that the alert queue is actually being worked.
B. None. A false positive is a non-event, and recording more than the closure wastes time.
C. Feedback for detection engineering and a training case for newer analysts on the team.
D. Performance material: documented closes are how analyst throughput gets measured.
column2:
C. Feedback for detection engineering and a training case for newer analysts on the team.

Closed false positives, well documented, point at where the detection logic could be sharper and help newer analysts learn what to look for. The methodology treats them as contributions, not as non-events.

column1:
An investigation checked for persistence mechanisms and found none. Under time pressure, the analyst leaves that check out of the record, reasoning that there was nothing to report. What went wrong?

A. Negative findings are evidence too: what was checked and ruled out bounds the case.
B. Nothing. Records document findings, and a check that found nothing produced no finding.
C. The real error came earlier: a persistence check at all means the case needed escalation.
D. Only the placement. Ruled-out checks belong in the appendix, not the main record.
column2:
A. Negative findings are evidence too: what was checked and ruled out bounds the case.

Omitting negative findings is one of the classic documentation pitfalls. 'Persistence checked: none found, here is what was examined' is what lets a reviewer trust the closure, lets the case re-open without re-doing the work, and defends the analyst if persistence later surfaces through a gap the check could not see. A record that only lists positive findings reads as an investigation that never looked.

column1:
An analyst pulls a suspicious binary off a host into a personal scratch directory while working the case, then uploads it to the case-management system at close. What happened to the artifact?

A. Nothing, as long as the file's contents did not change between acquisition and the upload.
B. It is fine if the analyst hashes the file at upload; that hash is what proves its integrity.
C. Nothing at triage. Chain of custody is IR's responsibility, and it only starts once the case escalates.
D. The chain of custody broke: nothing records who held the file, its hash, or access in that gap.
column2:
D. The chain of custody broke: nothing records who held the file, its hash, or access in that gap.

The chain is the continuous, time-stamped trail from acquisition onward: identifier, acquisition details, every transfer with re-verification, access log, disposal. A personal scratch directory is one of the most common silent breaks: the analyst held the file the whole time, but nothing documents that stretch. A hash at upload proves nothing about the gap before it; the hash has to be recorded at acquisition and re-verified at each move. In practice a gap usually goes to the weight the evidence carries rather than automatic exclusion, but it invites challenge. And custody starts at acquisition, not escalation: if the case might end with IR or external counsel, treat every artifact as evidence from the moment it is collected.

column1:
A closure record includes full log excerpts containing customer PII, on the reasoning that the excerpts are the evidence. What does the standard say?

A. Keep them. Inside a security system of record, completeness outranks the privacy question.
B. Drop the excerpts and describe them in prose; raw logs never belong in the record at all.
C. Sanitize what it does not need: a record can be complete and still be a data exposure.
D. Encrypt the record at rest; once it is encrypted, the PII question no longer applies.
column2:
C. Sanitize what it does not need: a record can be complete and still be a data exposure.

Sanitization mistakes are a named pitfall: a record that copies PII, regulated data, or sensitive operational detail into places that do not need it is complete and a data exposure at the same time. The appendix standard is log excerpts sanitized as needed, with the originals preserved under access control and chain of custody where they belong. Dropping the evidence entirely fails in the other direction, and encryption at rest does not change who can read the record through the system it lives in.

column1:
A record reads: 'powershell.exe (parent explorer.exe) started at 09:11:41 UTC on laptop-finance-09, one second after a RunMRU write, indicating paste-and-run initial access.' What does the clarity standard say about this sentence?

A. It is exactly right. One sentence carrying observation and conclusion is efficient documentation.
B. Split and label it: the process event is a fact, the initial-access reading is analysis.
C. Delete the second half. Analysis belongs to IR, and a triage record holds facts only.
D. The problem is voice, not content: rewrite it in the passive voice for objectivity.
column2:
B. Split and label it: the process event is a fact, the initial-access reading is analysis.

The first half is a fact: observable, timestamped, checkable against telemetry. The second half is analysis, a reading of the fact that could change. The standard asks for both, labeled as which is which, so a reviewer can revisit the analysis when new evidence lands without re-litigating the facts. Fused together, a wrong conclusion contaminates a correct observation. Triage records absolutely include analysis (that reasoning is what the replay test depends on), and the voice rule points the other way: active voice, naming who did what.

column1:
A closed case record contains a flawless technical timeline and nothing else. Who is left unserved?

A. Nobody. The timeline is the record; every other audience can derive what they need from it.
B. Only incident response, because a timeline without containment steps cannot be actioned.
C. Only legal, because a timeline without chain-of-custody entries is inadmissible as evidence in court.
D. Nearly every later reader: a timeline alone has no verdict, scope, business impact, or rationale.
column2:
D. Nearly every later reader: a timeline alone has no verdict, scope, business impact, or rationale.

The standards page names the readers: the timeline and origin-and-scope sections carry the next analyst, while business impact and lessons learned carry leadership and auditors. A timeline alone gives the next analyst only part of the investigation, and gives an executive, auditor, or trainer almost nothing: no business-impact translation, no decision rationale or approvals, no reasoning that connects evidence to verdict. Each layer is short; what matters is that the record is written knowing that most of its future readers are not the analyst who wrote it.

column1:
When in the lifecycle should Documentation begin?

A. At Alert. The record is built continuously; the final phase finalizes it.
B. At the end of the case. D is the seventh phase, and phases run in order.
C. At the Escalation decision, once the case is confirmed real and worth a record.
D. At Risk, once the verdict exists to structure the record around.
column2:
A. At Alert. The record is built continuously; the final phase finalizes it.

D is the closure gate for a record built continuously from Alert. Observations, decisions, and actions are captured in real time as each phase runs; the Documentation phase is where that living record is finalized into the durable, audit-quality artifact. Delaying the writing until after resolution loses detail and invites post-hoc rationalization, the exact failure the pitfalls page opens with.

column1:
A decision header labels the whole case 'High confidence'. The execution chain is corroborated by two independent sources; the attribution rests on a single hash match. What does the confidence rubric object to?

A. Nothing that rounding cannot fix: drop the whole case to Medium to stay conservative.
B. The label is redundant: confidence is already captured in the likelihood rating.
C. Label the claims, not the case: the chain is High and the attribution is Low.
D. Nothing. High is right, because the strongest evidence in the case sets the label.
column2:
C. Label the claims, not the case: the chain is High and the attribution is Low.

The rubric's first rule is to label the claim, not the case. A record usually carries several claims at different confidence levels, and one case-level label hides exactly what the next reader needs: here the execution chain is High (direct, corroborated, alternatives ruled out) and the attribution is Low (one indicator). Rounding the whole case down hides the same information in the other direction. And confidence is recorded beside likelihood, not folded into it: likelihood is how probable it is that the activity is malicious, confidence is how well the evidence supports that judgment.

column1:
A benign true positive closes on a signed vendor binary. Where and how should the binary's hash be recorded?

A. Leave it out. A benign close has no indicators, so the hash has no place in the record.
B. In section 06, marked known-good, so it feeds the allowlist and never the IOC feed.
C. In section 06 as an indicator of compromise, so future hunts find every host running it.
D. Only in the appendix log excerpts, where analysts will find it if the alert fires again.
column2:
B. In section 06, marked known-good, so it feeds the allowlist and never the IOC feed.

Section 06 is Indicators and observables, and every entry carries a disposition: malicious, suspicious, or known-good. A hash filed without that label tends to migrate into the intel platform, a blocklist, or a hunt query, and then every developer running the same signed tool matches a 'known incident artifact.' Leaving it out loses evidence the close rests on, and burying it in an appendix hides it from the correlation that should find it. Recording it as known-good keeps it findable and routes it to the allowlist or warninglist.

column1:
A Level 1 case on one ordinary-privilege host closes as benign-confirmed after a 25-minute pass. No pattern entry covers it. The analyst opens the nine-section event report to write it up. What does the template guidance say?

A. Keep it: every close gets the nine-section report, whatever depth the case ran at.
B. Use the five-field pattern-close record, since a benign close is what Level 0 records.
C. Use the alert report, written as the case ran and finalized at close.
D. No template is needed: a benign Level 1 close only needs the ticket's close code.
column2:
C. Use the alert report, written as the case ran and finalized at close.

Depth decides the artifact. Level 1 uses the alert report, written as you go and finalized at close, with the verdict on both axes and the reasoning behind the close. The nine-section event report is for Level 2 cases and every escalation. The five-field record needs a matching, current pattern entry, which this case does not have. And a bare close code is the 'just a false positive' shrug the methodology refuses: every close, at every depth, leaves a record someone can replay.
